outline: 68 Projectile Motion and Velocity as a Vector
190 Deriving the Six Equations of Motion

examples.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin with initial speed $V$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Its displacement is $\mathbf{r}(t)=Vt\cos\theta\,\mathbf{i}+(Vt\sin\theta-5t^2)\mathbf{j}$ metres. After $2$ seconds, its position vector is $24\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j}$ metres. Find its initial velocity vector, speed and angle of projection. Give the angle to $1$ decimal place.
examples.solution_text:
Substitute the known time and position into both components.
$\begin{aligned}24&=2V\cos\theta\\V\cos\theta&=12\\12&=2V\sin\theta-5(2)^2\\32&=2V\sin\theta\\V\sin\theta&=16\end{aligned}$
The initial velocity is $12\mathbf{i}+16\mathbf{j}\text{ m/s}$.
$\begin{aligned}V&=\sqrt{12^2+16^2}\\&=20\text{ m/s}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{12}\right)\\&\approx53.1^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal and returns to ground level after $4.8$ seconds. Its vertical displacement is $y=Vt\sin30^{\circ}-5t^2$ metres. Find its initial speed $V$.

A projectile is launched from level ground at $20\text{ m/s}$ and lands $20\text{ m}$ away. Its equations of motion are $x=20t\cos\theta$ and $y=20t\sin\theta-5t^2$. Find both possible angles of projection, where $0^{\circ}<\theta<90^{\circ}$.
examples.solution_text:
At landing, $y=0$. Use the positive time of flight.
$\begin{aligned}0&=t(20\sin\theta-5t)\\t&=4\sin\theta\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the horizontal equation.
$\begin{aligned}20&=20\cos\theta(4\sin\theta)\\20&=40\sin2\theta\\\sin2\theta&=\frac12\\2\theta&=30^{\circ}\text{ or }150^{\circ}\\\theta&=15^{\circ}\text{ or }75^{\circ}\end{aligned}$
Both angles give positive flight times and the required range.

Sea level is $y=-45$ relative to the pipe.
$\begin{aligned}-45&=-5t^2\\t^2&=9\\t&=3\text{ s}\end{aligned}$
Use the positive time in $x=Vt$.
$\begin{aligned}18&=3V\\V&=6\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$

Solve the horizontal equation for the time at the wall.
$\begin{aligned}30&=Vt\cos45^{\circ}\\t&=\frac{30}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the vertical equation at $y=10$.
$\begin{aligned}10&=V\sin45^{\circ}\left(\frac{30}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\right)-5\left(\frac{30}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\right)^2\\10&=30-\frac{9000}{V^2}\\\frac{9000}{V^2}&=20\\V^2&=450\\V&=15\sqrt2\text{ m/s}\\&\approx21.2\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$
The time at the wall is $2\text{ s}$, and its positive height places it within the flight.

examples.question_text: A particle is projected from the origin at $40\text{ m/s}$ and passes through $(40,25)$, with distances in metres. Its equations are $x=40t\cos\theta$ and $y=40t\sin\theta-5t^2$. Find both possible angles of projection to $1$ decimal place, where $0^{\circ}<\theta<90^{\circ}$.
examples.solution_text:
Solve the horizontal equation for $t$.
$\begin{aligned}40&=40t\cos\theta\\t&=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the vertical equation and use $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$.
$\begin{aligned}25&=40\sin\theta\left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)-5\left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)^2\\25&=40\tan\theta-5\sec^2\theta\\25&=40\tan\theta-5(1+\tan^2\theta)\\\tan^2\theta-8\tan\theta+6&=0\\\tan\theta&=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{64-24}}{2}\\&=4\pm\sqrt{10}\\\theta&\approx40.0^{\circ}\text{ or }82.1^{\circ}\end{aligned}$
Both angles have positive horizontal velocity, give positive times and reach the point above ground during the flight.

examples.question_text: A ball is launched from level ground at $30\text{ m/s}$ and reaches a greatest height of $20\text{ m}$. Its vertical velocity and displacement are $\dot y=30\sin\theta-10t$ and $y=30t\sin\theta-5t^2$. Find its angle of projection to $1$ decimal place, where $0^{\circ}<\theta<90^{\circ}$.
examples.solution_text:
At greatest height, the vertical velocity is zero.
$\begin{aligned}0&=30\sin\theta-10t\\t&=3\sin\theta\end{aligned}$
Substitute this time into the height equation.
$\begin{aligned}20&=30\sin\theta(3\sin\theta)-5(3\sin\theta)^2\\20&=45\sin^2\theta\\\sin^2\theta&=\frac49\\\sin\theta&=\frac23\\\theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac23\right)\\&\approx41.8^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

Solve the horizontal equation at landing for $t$.
$\begin{aligned}20&=Vt\cos45^{\circ}\\t&=\frac{20}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\end{aligned}$
The sea is at $y=-65$. Substitute the time into the vertical equation.
$\begin{aligned}-65&=-V\sin45^{\circ}\left(\frac{20}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\right)-5\left(\frac{20}{V\cos45^{\circ}}\right)^2\\-65&=-20-\frac{4000}{V^2}\\\frac{4000}{V^2}&=45\\V^2&=\frac{800}{9}\\V&=\frac{20\sqrt2}{3}\text{ m/s}\\&\approx9.4\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$
The landing time is $3\text{ s}$. The stone moves downwards throughout, so this is its first contact with sea level.

examples.derivation: At t=2, the horizontal component gives ux=24/2=12 and the vertical component gives uy=(12+20)/2=16. Initial velocity is 12i+16j m/s, speed is sqrt(144+256)=20 m/s, and angle is arctan(16/12)=53.1 degrees. This follows source lines 1677–1699.
Landing gives 0=4.8V(1/2)-5(4.8)^2=2.4V-115.2, hence V=48 m/s. The specified time is positive. This follows source lines 1636–1648.

The nonzero landing root is t=4sin(theta). Substitution into x=20 gives 20=80sin(theta)cos(theta)=40sin(2theta). Thus sin(2theta)=1/2 and the admissible angles are 15 and 75 degrees. Both have positive flight times. This follows source lines 2566–2589.

At sea level, -45=-5t^2, giving the positive time t=3 s. Then 18=3V gives V=6 m/s. The planar diagram correctly shows horizontal launch, the vertical drop and horizontal distance, without revealing the answer. This follows source lines 1359–1370.

At x=30, t=30/(Vcos45). Substituting y=10 gives 10=30-9000/V^2, hence V^2=450 and V=15sqrt(2)=21.2 m/s to one decimal place. The corresponding time is 2 s. The planar diagram shows the correct launch angle and wall dimensions. This follows source lines 1998–2023.

At x=40, t=sec(theta). Then 25=40tan(theta)-5sec^2(theta), giving tan^2(theta)-8tan(theta)+6=0. Its roots are 4±sqrt(10), yielding 40.0 and 82.1 degrees to one decimal place. Both roots are positive, and y=25 is reached before ground landing. This follows the substitution and tangent-quadratic method in source lines 1902–1930.

Zero vertical velocity gives t=3sin(theta). Substitution into maximum height gives 20=90sin^2(theta)-45sin^2(theta), so sin^2(theta)=4/9. The specified acute angle has sin(theta)=2/3, giving theta=41.8 degrees. This follows source lines 1743–1766.

At x=20, t=20/(Vcos45). With sea level y=-65, substitution gives -65=-20-4000/V^2. Therefore V^2=800/9 and V=20sqrt(2)/3=9.4 m/s to one decimal place. The landing time is 3 s; vertical velocity remains negative throughout. The planar diagram correctly shows downward projection and the given distances. This follows source lines 2622–2657.
